title: More than the oceans
hookLine: the tears shed over countless lives are more than the four oceans (SN 15.3)

lines: A HARD CRY HAS A SHAPE.
cards: A hard cry has a shape. Where you were sitting. What the light looked like.
The way it came in waves, and how tired the body was after. A death, maybe, or a breakup, or a phone call. In the middle of it, a loss can seem like the only one in the world.
In a short chapter of the Connected Sayings about the long round of lives, the Buddha takes that one private cry and sets it beside a very large body of water.

teach.b: SN 15.3 is a question and answer. The Buddha asks the monks: which is more?
The tears you have shed while wandering this long round, weeping and wailing because you were joined with what you disliked and parted from what you loved, or the water in the four great oceans?
The monks answer from what they've been taught: the tears, sir. The tears are more. Yes, the Buddha says, and he names them one by one.

teach.h: A MOTHER, A FATHER, A CHILD
teach.b: For a long time you have suffered the death of a mother. The tears shed over that alone are more than the four oceans. The death of a father.
A brother. A sister. A son.
A daughter. The loss of relatives, of wealth, the suffering of illness. Each time, the same refrain: more than the water in the four great oceans.
It's a hard teaching to sit with, and the text doesn't soften it. But notice its tone. It isn't scolding anyone for crying.
It's almost tender: you've lost so much, for so long.
It takes grief seriously enough to measure it against the sea. Then it draws a conclusion: enough.
Reason enough to grow weary of the round, to let the craving that keeps it turning fade, and to be free. Buddhists hold the idea of many lives in different ways.
Some take rebirth literally; some modern teachers read it more as moment to moment. Either way, the picture makes one point plainly: in this teaching, no grief is the first.

how: Buddhist communities mark grief in many ways, with chanting, merit-making and memorial rites for the dead, and teachings like the tears and the oceans are sometimes shared at funerals and in times of loss.

p: joined with the disliked, parted from the loved

s: the Buddha scolds the monks for crying
the tone is almost tender: it measures grief against the sea and takes it seriously.
the sutta names the deaths of mothers, fathers, brothers, sisters, sons and daughters
each with the same refrain: more than the four great oceans.
there is only one Buddhist reading of the many lives in this teaching
some take rebirth literally; some modern teachers read it more as moment to moment.

games.q: the Buddha asks you: which is more, the tears you've shed over the long round, or the water in the four great oceans? what do you answer?
games.why: the monks answer the tears, and the Buddha agrees, naming each kind of loss in turn.

practice: If it feels right, let one old grief come to mind, not the rawest one if that's too much, and let it sit beside you like an old friend, without pushing it away or digging into it.

Breathe with it, and widen the picture a little: so many people, across so much time, have felt exactly this; let that be company, not a burden. If it's too heavy, come back to the breath at any time.

wordCard.voice: Assu. The Pali word for a tear, in SN 15.3, where the tears shed over loss across the long round are more than the water in the four great oceans. Today's word.

orig.note: Pali assu: a tear. SN 15.3 is the Assu Sutta.

carryVoice: Your line: be gentle with grief. Whoever is grieving, someone near you or you yourself, deserves that gentleness. Day six hundred forty-nine.
